candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 1:1-3, trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon, 1912). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

1 Enoch opens with a programmatic blessing 'which Enoch blessed the elect and righteous, who will be living in the day of tribulation, when all the wicked and godless are to be removed' (Charles 1912 trans.). The opening immediately establishes the book's apocalyptic-eschatological orientation: it is written for the persecuted righteous of a future tribulation, not as historical narrative but as prophetic vision. The Tewahedo canonical reception locates this opening alongside the Pentateuchal openings as setting the entire revelatory horizon — the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok is read liturgically in Tewahedo Lenten cycles precisely for this eschatological orientation.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 1:3-4, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'The Holy Great One will come forth from His dwelling, and the eternal God will tread upon the earth, even on Mount Sinai, and appear in the strength of His might from the heaven of heavens' — the Sinai theophany extended to a general theological pattern. The God who once came down on Sinai will come again at the eschaton; the historical theophany prefigures the eschatological. The Tewahedo Synaxarium readings for the Feast of the Transfiguration explicitly connect this verse to the Tabor manifestation: each visible coming of the Most High to creation participates in the one cosmic visitation that the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok foretells.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 1:9, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Jude 1:14-15 quoting this verse verbatim.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'Behold, He cometh with ten thousands of His saints to execute judgment upon all, and to destroy all the ungodly' is the verse the New Testament Jude 1:14-15 quotes VERBATIM, attributing it to 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam'. Jude's canonical-NT quotation of 1 Enoch as inspired prophecy is the strongest textual basis for the Tewahedo canon's reception of 1 Enoch as Scripture — if Jude treats 1 Enoch as prophetic Word, the Tewahedo argues, the rest of the Church should at least not deny what an apostle affirmed. This verse is therefore THE textual bridge between 1 Enoch and the canonical New Testament.
